answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1533–1592 · French essayist, magistrate & mayor of Bordeaux
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. The sentence comes from Montaigne’s essay Of Friendship (Essais, Book I, first published 1580), where he is writing about his dead friend Étienne de La Boétie. This exact English wording is Charles Cotton’s translation as revised by William Carew Hazlitt — confirmed word for word in the 1877 text at Project Gutenberg ↗.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Charles Cotton (1685), revised by William Carew Hazlitt (1877)
Printed as XXVII in the Cotton–Hazlitt edition; numbered 28 in modern French editions

source.excerpt: But in the friendship I speak of, they mix and work themselves into one piece, with so universal a mixture, that there is no more sign of the seam by which they were first conjoined. If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I. There is, beyond all that I am able to say, I know not what inexplicable and fated power that brought on this union.
trail: 1580 — the French. Montaigne publishes the Essais; “De l’amitié” carries the sentence as “Si on me presse de dire pourquoy je l’aymois… Par ce que c’estoit luy ; par ce que c’estoit moy” ↗.
1603 — the first English. John Florio renders it “If a man urge me to tell wherefore I loved him, I feele it can not be expressed…” — Florio’s Book I, chapter 27 ↗.

1685, revised 1877 — the wording people quote. Charles Cotton’s translation, revised by William Carew Hazlitt, gives the “importune” phrasing; HyperEssays names the translation ↗ and the Project Gutenberg text ↗ carries it verbatim in chapter XXVII.

Today. Wikiquote ↗ pairs the French original with an English rendering and lists both the Florio and the “importune” wordings as variants under Book I, ch. 28 — a useful reminder that the sentence has no single canonical English form.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Cotton translation edited by William Carew Hazlitt, chapter XXVII, “Of Friendship.” The “him” is Étienne de La Boétie, who had been dead since 1563 when Montaigne wrote this.

source.rightsNote: Everything in play here is long out of copyright in the United States. The French Essais first appeared in 1580, Florio’s English translation in 1603, and the Charles Cotton translation quoted above in the revision edited by William Carew Hazlitt in 1877 — all far earlier than the 1931 threshold, which is why the full text is freely readable at Project Gutenberg ↗. Note that modern twentieth-century translations of the same sentence are not public domain; the wording on this page is the pre-1931 one.

author.name: Michel de Montaigne
author.heading: The man who invented the essay
author.metaLine: 1533–1592 · French essayist, magistrate and mayor of Bordeaux
author.bio: Michel de Montaigne (28 February 1533 – 13 September 1592) was a French magistrate who retired to his tower library and, by writing down whatever crossed his mind, more or less invented the personal essay. His Essais first appeared in 1580 and he kept expanding them until his death; Wikipedia notes ↗ that in his own lifetime he was admired more as a statesman — he served in the Bordeaux Parlement and as the city’s mayor — than as an author. The friendship recorded in this quote was with Étienne de La Boétie, a fellow magistrate three years his senior who died in 1563.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The authorship is not in doubt — this really is Montaigne. What goes wrong is everything downstream of that: quote sites strip the work, the chapter and the translator, then print whichever of four competing English versions they happened to copy, all under the same bare byline.

items.why: The Goodreads entry ↗ for this line names no book, no chapter and no translator — and prints a further variant again (“If any one should importune me… inexplicable and inevitable power”) rather than the Cotton–Hazlitt text.

items.who: Cotton’s English, presented as Montaigne’s own phrasing
items.why: Montaigne wrote in French: “Si on me presse de dire pourquoy je l’aymois… Par ce que c’estoit luy ; par ce que c’estoit moy” ↗. The word “importune” is a translator’s choice, not Montaigne’s.

items.who: John Florio’s 1603 version, run under the same byline
items.why: BrainyQuote ↗ carries “If a man urge me to tell wherefore I loved him… because it was myself” with no translator named — that phrasing traces to Florio’s 1603 English ↗, a different translation entirely.

The Cotton–Hazlitt edition prints it as CHAPTER XXVII, “Of Friendship” ↗, matching Wikipedia’s chapter list ↗; modern French editions and Wikiquote ↗ number the same essay 28. Neither citation is an error.

misattribution.truthLine: Montaigne wrote it, in French, in Of Friendship, about Étienne de La Boétie — and the English everyone quotes is Charles Cotton’s, as revised by William Carew Hazlitt, readable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗.

context.heading: Four years, and the rest was smoke
lead: Montaigne is not writing an aphorism about friendship in general. He is writing about one person: Étienne de La Boétie, a fellow magistrate at the Bordeaux Parlement who died in 1563. The essay says the two men had somehow recognised each other before they ever met — “We sought one another long before we met” — and that after his friend’s death, weighed against “the four years I had the happiness to enjoy the sweet society of this excellent man,” the whole of the rest of his comfortable life was “nothing but smoke, an obscure and tedious night.”

The famous line is what he reaches for when analysis fails him. He has just described two souls mixed so completely that there is “no more sign of the seam by which they were first conjoined,” and the sentence immediately after the quote admits defeat outright: “There is, beyond all that I am able to say, I know not what inexplicable and fated power that brought on this union.” The line is a shrug, not a maxim — which is exactly why it survives being pulled out of context better than most.
context.detailsSummary: Why the wording changes from site to site
detailsBody: Montaigne wrote in French. Every English version you have ever seen of this line is somebody’s translation, and the choices differ sharply. John Florio’s 1603 rendering — the one Shakespeare’s generation read — gives “If a man urge me to tell wherefore I loved him, I feele it can not be expressed, but by answering; Because it was he, because it was my selfe.”

The wording asked about here is the Charles Cotton line as revised by William Carew Hazlitt, which is the version that dominates the internet because it is the one Project Gutenberg digitised. Shorter modern renderings — “If you press me to say why I loved him…” — are different translations again. None of them is wrong; they are just not interchangeable, and quote sites almost never say which one they are printing.
